For each Technique and SubTechnique identified in q2, find all Mitigation nodes connected to them via the MITIGATES relationship. Return the Mitigation id, name, and the linked Technique/SubTechnique.

queries: MATCH (n:SubTechnique) WHERE coalesce(n.attack_id, n.id) IN $ids OPTIONAL MATCH (n)-[r]-(m) WITH n, CASE WHEN m IS NULL THEN NULL ELSE type(r) END AS rel, CASE WHEN m IS NULL THEN NULL ELSE startNode(r) = n END AS outgoing, CASE WHEN m IS NULL THEN NULL ELSE head(labels(m)) END AS neighbour_label, count(m) AS cnt WITH n, collect(CASE WHEN rel IS NULL THEN NULL ELSE {rel: rel, outgoing: outgoing, label: neighbour_label, count: cnt} END) AS raw WITH n, [f IN raw WHERE f IS NOT NULL] AS facets RETURN coalesce(n.attack_id, n.id) AS id, n.name AS name, n.properties_json AS properties_json, facets AS facets LIMIT 1000

MATCH (t:SubTechnique) WHERE t.attack_id IN $ids OPTIONAL MATCH (t)<-[:MITIGATES]-(m:Mitigation) RETURN t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name, m.attack_id AS mitigation_id, m.name AS mitigation_name LIMIT 1000

MATCH (t:SubTechnique) WHERE t.attack_id IN $ids OPTIONAL MATCH (t)<-[:MITIGATES]-(m:Mitigation) RETURN t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name, m.attack_id AS mitigation_id, m.name AS mitigation_name LIMIT 1000

MATCH (t:Technique)-[:HAS_SUBTECHNIQUE]->(st:SubTechnique) WHERE t.attack_id IN $ids OR st.attack_id IN $ids RETURN t.attack_id AS parent_id, t.name AS parent_name, st.attack_id AS subtechnique_id, st.name AS subtechnique_name LIMIT 1000

MATCH (ta:Tactic)-[:HAS_TECHNIQUE]->(t) WHERE (t:Technique OR t:SubTechnique) AND t.attack_id IN $ids RETURN t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name, ta.attack_id AS in_tactic_id, ta.name AS in_tactic_name LIMIT 1000
g.V().has("id", within(ids)).project("ap","tax").by(elementMap()).by(__.out("MAPS_TO").hasLabel("TaxonomyEntry").has("taxonomy_name","ATTACK").elementMap().fold()).limit(1000)

plan.text: Find all AttackPattern nodes that have an EXPLOITS_WEAKNESS relationship to a Weakness node representing CWE-287. For each matching AttackPattern, retrieve (a) all Mitigation nodes connected via HAS_MITIGATION, and (b) all TaxonomyEntry nodes connected via MAPS_TO where the taxonomy is ATT&CK (to obtain the corresponding ATT&CK technique IDs).

Find all Technique and SubTechnique nodes whose attack_id matches the ATT&CK technique IDs obtained from the CAPEC TaxonomyEntry mappings (via the attack-technique-id join). For each matching Technique/SubTechnique, retrieve all Mitigation nodes connected via the MITIGATES relationship.

queries: MATCH (t) WHERE (t:Technique OR t:SubTechnique) AND t.attack_id IN $ids OPTIONAL MATCH (t)<-[:MITIGATES]-(m:Mitigation) RETURN t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name, m.attack_id AS mitigation_id, m.name AS mitigation_name LIMIT 1000

g.V().hasLabel("Weakness").has("id", within(cweIds)).as("w").in("EXPLOITS_WEAKNESS").hasLabel("AttackPattern").as("ap").project("w","ap","tax").by(__.select("w").elementMap()).by(__.select("ap").elementMap()).by(__.out("MAPS_TO").hasLabel("TaxonomyEntry").has("taxonomy_name","ATTACK").elementMap().fold()).limit(1000)

claims: CAPEC-168 (Windows ::DATA Alternate Data Stream) description: An attacker exploits the functionality of Microsoft NTFS Alternate Data Streams (ADS) to undermine system security. ADS allows multiple "files" to be stored in one directory entry referenced as filename:streamname. One or more alternate data streams may be stored in any file or directory. Normal Microsoft utilities do not show the presence of an ADS stream attached to a file. The additional space for the ADS is not recorded in the displayed file size. The additional space for ADS is accounted for in the used space on the volume. An ADS can be any type of file. ADS are copied by standard Microsoft utilities between NTFS volumes. ADS can be used by an attacker or intruder to hide tools, scripts, and data from detection by normal system utilities. Many anti-virus programs do not check for or scan ADS. Windows Vista does have a switch (-R) on the command line DIR command that will display alternate streams..

queries: MATCH (n) WHERE (n:Analytic OR n:Campaign OR n:DataComponent OR n:DetectionStrategy OR n:Group OR n:Matrix OR n:Mitigation OR n:Software OR n:SubTechnique OR n:Tactic OR n:Technique) AND any(term IN $names WHERE toLower(n.name) CONTAINS term) WITH collect(n) AS cand WITH cand, [x IN cand WHERE any(t IN $names WHERE toLower(x.name) = t)] AS exact UNWIND (CASE WHEN size(exact) > 0 THEN exact ELSE cand END) AS n OPTIONAL MATCH (n)-[r]-(m) WITH n, CASE WHEN m IS NULL THEN NULL ELSE type(r) END AS rel, CASE WHEN m IS NULL THEN NULL ELSE startNode(r) = n END AS outgoing, CASE WHEN m IS NULL THEN NULL ELSE head(labels(m)) END AS neighbour_label, count(m) AS cnt WITH n, collect(CASE WHEN rel IS NULL THEN NULL ELSE {rel: rel, outgoing: outgoing, label: neighbour_label, count: cnt} END) AS raw WITH n, [f IN raw WHERE f IS NOT NULL] AS facets RETURN coalesce(n.attack_id, n.id) AS id, n.name AS name, n.properties_json AS properties_json, facets AS facets LIMIT 1000

claims: CAPEC-1 (Accessing Functionality Not Properly Constrained by ACLs) description: In applications, particularly web applications, access to functionality is mitigated by an authorization framework. This framework maps Access Control Lists (ACLs) to elements of the application's functionality; particularly URL's for web apps. In the case that the administrator failed to specify an ACL for a particular element, an attacker may be able to access it with impunity. An attacker with the ability to access functionality not properly constrained by ACLs can obtain sensitive information and possibly compromise the entire application. Such an attacker can access resources that must be available only to users at a higher privilege level, can access management sections of the application, or can run queries for data that they otherwise not supposed to..
CAPEC-1 (Accessing Functionality Not Properly Constrained by ACLs) has 1 ATT&CK mapping: T1574.010.

CAPEC-10 (Buffer Overflow via Environment Variables) description: This attack pattern involves causing a buffer overflow through manipulation of environment variables. Once the adversary finds that they can modify an environment variable, they may try to overflow associated buffers. This attack leverages implicit trust often placed in environment variables..

CAPEC-100 (Overflow Buffers) description: Buffer Overflow attacks target improper or missing bounds checking on buffer operations, typically triggered by input injected by an adversary. As a consequence, an adversary is able to write past the boundaries of allocated buffer regions in memory, causing a program crash or potentially redirection of execution as per the adversaries' choice..

CAPEC-101 (Server Side Include (SSI) Injection) description: An attacker can use Server Side Include (SSI) Injection to send code to a web application that then gets executed by the web server. Doing so enables the attacker to achieve similar results to Cross Site Scripting, viz., arbitrary code execution and information disclosure, albeit on a more limited scale, since the SSI directives are nowhere near as powerful as a full-fledged scripting language. Nonetheless, the attacker can conveniently gain access to sensitive files, such as password files, and execute shell commands..
CAPEC-11 (Cause Web Server Misclassification) has 1 ATT&CK mapping: T1036.006.
CAPEC-112 (Brute Force) has 1 ATT&CK mapping: T1110.
CAPEC-114 (Authentication Abuse) has 1 ATT&CK mapping: T1548.
CAPEC-115 (Authentication Bypass) has 1 ATT&CK mapping: T1548.

CAPEC-62 (Cross Site Request Forgery) description: An attacker crafts malicious web links and distributes them (via web pages, email, etc.), typically in a targeted manner, hoping to induce users to click on the link and execute the malicious action against some third-party application. If successful, the action embedded in the malicious link will be processed and accepted by the targeted application with the users' privilege level. This type of attack leverages the persistence and implicit trust placed in user session cookies by many web applications today. In such an architecture, once the user authenticates to an application and a session cookie is created on the user's system, all following transactions for that session are authenticated using that cookie including potential actions initiated by an attacker and simply "riding" the existing session cookie..
CAPEC-620 (Drop Encryption Level) description: An attacker forces the encryption level to be lowered, thus enabling a successful attack against the encrypted data..
CAPEC-620 (Drop Encryption Level) has 1 ATT&CK mapping: T1600.

CAPEC-621 (Analysis of Packet Timing and Sizes) description: An attacker may intercept and log encrypted transmissions for the purpose of analyzing metadata such as packet timing and sizes. Although the actual data may be encrypted, this metadata may reveal valuable information to an attacker. Note that this attack is applicable to VOIP data as well as application data, especially for interactive apps that require precise timing and low-latency (e.g. thin-clients)..

CAPEC-622 (Electromagnetic Side-Channel Attack) description: In this attack scenario, the attacker passively monitors electromagnetic emanations that are produced by the targeted electronic device as an unintentional side-effect of its processing. From these emanations, the attacker derives information about the data that is being processed (e.g. the attacker can recover cryptographic keys by monitoring emanations associated with cryptographic processing). This style of attack requires proximal access to the device, however attacks have been demonstrated at public conferences that work at distances of up to 10-15 feet. There have not been any significant studies to determine the maximum practical distance for such attacks. Since the attack is passive, it is nearly impossible to detect and the targeted device will continue to operate as normal after a successful attack..

CAPEC-623 (Compromising Emanations Attack) description: Compromising Emanations (CE) are defined as unintentional signals which an attacker may intercept and analyze to disclose the information processed by the targeted equipment. Commercial mobile devices and retransmission devices have displays, buttons, microchips, and radios that emit mechanical emissions in the form of sound or vibrations. Capturing these emissions can help an adversary understand what the device is doing..

CAPEC-624 (Hardware Fault Injection) description: The adversary uses disruptive signals or events, or alters the physical environment a device operates in, to cause faulty behavior in electronic devices. This can include electromagnetic pulses, laser pulses, clock glitches, ambient temperature extremes, and more. When performed in a controlled manner on devices performing cryptographic operations, this faulty behavior can be exploited to derive secret key information..

queries: MATCH (n:Technique) WHERE coalesce(n.attack_id, n.id) IN $ids OPTIONAL MATCH (n)-[r]-(m) WITH n, CASE WHEN m IS NULL THEN NULL ELSE type(r) END AS rel, CASE WHEN m IS NULL THEN NULL ELSE startNode(r) = n END AS outgoing, CASE WHEN m IS NULL THEN NULL ELSE head(labels(m)) END AS neighbour_label, count(m) AS cnt WITH n, collect(CASE WHEN rel IS NULL THEN NULL ELSE {rel: rel, outgoing: outgoing, label: neighbour_label, count: cnt} END) AS raw WITH n, [f IN raw WHERE f IS NOT NULL] AS facets RETURN coalesce(n.attack_id, n.id) AS id, n.name AS name, n.properties_json AS properties_json, facets AS facets LIMIT 1000

Retrieve AttackPatterns whose description or AlternateTerm indicates undermining, bypassing, disabling, or evading security controls and defensive tooling (e.g., disabling antivirus, tampering with logs, disabling audit). For each, return its Mitigations, Consequences, and ExecutionSteps so the analyst sees the full attack flow and recommended countermeasures.

queries: MATCH (t) WHERE (t:Technique OR t:SubTechnique) AND t.attack_id IN $ids OPTIONAL MATCH (t)<-[:MITIGATES]-(m:Mitigation) RETURN t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name, m.attack_id AS mitigation_id, m.name AS mitigation_name LIMIT 1000
g.V().hasLabel("AttackPattern").project("ap","tax").by(elementMap()).by(__.out("MAPS_TO").hasLabel("TaxonomyEntry").has("taxonomy_name","ATTACK").elementMap().fold()).limit(1000)

plan.text: Retrieve all Techniques and SubTechniques under the 'Impair Defenses' tactic (TA0008), including any related techniques for hiding artifacts (T1564) and data store or database manipulation (T1565) that let an attacker degrade or disable security controls so defenders cannot trust observables.

For each Technique and SubTechnique identified under Impair Defenses, Hide Artifacts, and Data Store or Database Manipulation, retrieve all Mitigations that MITIGATES those techniques, to surface defensive countermeasures.

For the same set of Impair Defenses / Hide Artifacts / Data Store Manipulation techniques, retrieve all DetectionStrategies that DETECT those techniques, and the Analytics (HAS_ANALYTIC) that implement each strategy, so defenders know how to observe the impairment.

Find AttackPatterns whose description involves disabling, degrading, or manipulating security controls, logging, or observables (e.g., disabling audit logs, modifying firewall rules, tampering with monitoring data). For each, retrieve associated Mitigations (HAS_MITIGATION), Consequences (HAS_CONSEQUENCE), and Indicators (HAS_INDICATOR).

queries: MATCH (t) WHERE (t:Technique OR t:SubTechnique) AND t.attack_id IN $ids MATCH (t)<-[:DETECTS]-(d:DetectionStrategy) OPTIONAL MATCH (d)-[:HAS_ANALYTIC]->(a:Analytic) RETURN t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name, d.attack_id AS detection_id, d.name AS detection_name, a.attack_id AS analytic_id, a.name AS analytic_name LIMIT 1000

MATCH (t:Technique) WHERE t.attack_id IN $ids OPTIONAL MATCH (t)<-[:MITIGATES]-(m:Mitigation) RETURN t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name, m.attack_id AS mitigation_id, m.name AS mitigation_name LIMIT 1000

MATCH (ta:Tactic)-[:HAS_TECHNIQUE]->(t) WHERE (t:Technique OR t:SubTechnique) AND t.attack_id IN $ids RETURN t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name, ta.attack_id AS in_tactic_id, ta.name AS in_tactic_name LIMIT 1000

T1021.001 (Remote Desktop Protocol): Adversaries may use Valid Accounts to log into a computer using the Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP). The adversary may then perform actions as the logged-on user.

Remote desktop is a common feature in operating systems. It allows a user to log into an interactive session with a system desktop graphical user interface on a remote system. Microsoft refers to its implementation of the Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) as Remote Desktop Services (RDS).(Citation: TechNet Remote Desktop Services) 

Adversaries may connect to a remote system over RDP/RDS to expand access if the service is enabled and allows access to accounts with known credentials.

CAPEC-168 (Windows ::DATA Alternate Data Stream): An attacker exploits the functionality of Microsoft NTFS Alternate Data Streams (ADS) to undermine system security. ADS allows multiple "files" to be stored in one directory entry referenced as filename:streamname. One or more alternate data streams may be stored in any file or directory. Normal Microsoft utilities do not show the presence of an ADS stream attached to a file. The additional space for the ADS is not recorded in the displayed file size. The additional space for ADS is accounted for in the used space on the volume. An ADS can be any type of file. ADS are copied by standard Microsoft utilities between NTFS volumes.

This ensures that only trusted and authorized code is executed, reducing the risk of malware and unauthorized actions. This mitigation can be implemented through the following measures:

Application Control:

- Use Case: Use tools like AppLocker or Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) to create whitelists of authorized applications and block unauthorized ones. On Linux, use tools like SELinux or AppArmor to define mandatory access control policies for application execution.
- Implementation: Allow only digitally signed or pre-approved applications to execute on servers and endpoints. (e.g., `New-AppLockerPolicy -PolicyType Enforced -FilePath "C:\Policies\AppLocker.xml"`) 


Script Blocking:

- Use Case: Use script control mechanisms to block unauthorized execution of scripts, such as PowerShell or JavaScript. Web Browsers: Use browser extensions or settings to block JavaScript execution from untrusted sources.
- Implementation: Configure PowerShell to enforce Constrained Language Mode for non-administrator users. (e.g., `Set-ExecutionPolicy AllSigned`) 

Executable Blocking:

- Use Case: Prevent execution of binaries from suspicious locations, such as `%TEMP%` or `%APPDATA%` directories.
- Implementation: Block execution of `.exe`, `.bat`, or `.ps1` files from user-writable directories.

Dynamic Analysis Prevention:
- Use Case: Use behavior-based execution prevention tools to identify and block malicious activity in real time.
- Implemenation: Employ EDR solutions that analyze runtime behavior and block suspicious code execution..

T1021.002 (SMB/Windows Admin Shares): Adversaries may use Valid Accounts to interact with a remote network share using Server Message Block (SMB). The adversary may then perform actions as the logged-on user.

SMB is a file, printer, and serial port sharing protocol for Windows machines on the same network or domain. Adversaries may use SMB to interact with file shares, allowing them to move laterally throughout a network. Linux and macOS implementations of SMB typically use Samba.

Windows systems have hidden network shares that are accessible only to administrators and provide the ability for remote file copy and other administrative functions. Example network shares include `C$`, `ADMIN$`, and `IPC$`.

CAPEC-163 (Spear Phishing): An adversary targets a specific user or group with a Phishing (CAPEC-98) attack tailored to a category of users in order to have maximum relevance and deceptive capability. Spear Phishing is an enhanced version of the Phishing attack targeted to a specific user or group. The quality of the targeted email is usually enhanced by appearing to come from a known or trusted entity. If the email account of some trusted entity has been compromised the message may be digitally signed. The message will contain information specific to the targeted users that will enhance the probability that they will follow the URL to the compromised site.

T1566.002 (Spearphishing Link): Adversaries may send spearphishing emails with a malicious link in an attempt to gain access to victim systems. Spearphishing with a link is a specific variant of spearphishing. It is different from other forms of spearphishing in that it employs the use of links to download malware contained in email, instead of attaching malicious files to the email itself, to avoid defenses that may inspect email attachments. Spearphishing may also involve social engineering techniques, such as posing as a trusted source.

All forms of spearphishing are electronically delivered social engineering targeted at a specific individual, company, or industry. In this case, the malicious emails contain links.

CAPEC-163 (Spear Phishing): An adversary targets a specific user or group with a Phishing (CAPEC-98) attack tailored to a category of users in order to have maximum relevance and deceptive capability. Spear Phishing is an enhanced version of the Phishing attack targeted to a specific user or group. The quality of the targeted email is usually enhanced by appearing to come from a known or trusted entity. If the email account of some trusted entity has been compromised the message may be digitally signed. The message will contain information specific to the targeted users that will enhance the probability that they will follow the URL to the compromised site.

CAPEC-164 (Mobile Phishing): An adversary targets mobile phone users with a phishing attack for the purpose of soliciting account passwords or sensitive information from the user. Mobile Phishing is a variation of the Phishing social engineering technique where the attack is initiated via a text or SMS message, rather than email. The user is enticed to provide information or visit a compromised web site via this message. Apart from the manner in which the attack is initiated, the attack proceeds as a standard Phishing attack.

CAPEC-656 (Voice Phishing): An adversary targets users with a phishing attack for the purpose of soliciting account passwords or sensitive information from the user. Voice Phishing is a variation of the Phishing social engineering technique where the attack is initiated via a voice call, rather than email. The user is enticed to provide sensitive information by the adversary, who masquerades as a legitimate employee of the alleged organization. Voice Phishing attacks deviate from standard Phishing attacks, in that a user doesn't typically interact with a compromised website to provide sensitive information and instead provides this information verbally.

CAPEC-564 (Run Software at Logon): Operating system allows logon scripts to be run whenever a specific user or users logon to a system. If adversaries can access these scripts, they may insert additional code into the logon script. This code can allow them to maintain persistence or move laterally within an enclave because it is executed every time the affected user or users logon to a computer. Modifying logon scripts can effectively bypass workstation and enclave firewalls. Depending on the access configuration of the logon scripts, either local credentials or a remote administrative account may be necessary.

CAPEC-564 (Run Software at Logon) has Abstraction: Detailed; Status: Draft.

CAPEC-564 (Run Software at Logon): Operating system allows logon scripts to be run whenever a specific user or users logon to a system. If adversaries can access these scripts, they may insert additional code into the logon script. This code can allow them to maintain persistence or move laterally within an enclave because it is executed every time the affected user or users logon to a computer. Modifying logon scripts can effectively bypass workstation and enclave firewalls. Depending on the access configuration of the logon scripts, either local credentials or a remote administrative account may be necessary.

plan.text: Find Technique and SubTechnique nodes whose description involves guessing widely used or factory-set login credentials to break into a system (e.g., password guessing, default/factory credentials, brute-force of common passwords).

Find AttackPattern nodes whose description or execution steps involve guessing widely used or factory-set login credentials to gain system access, and retrieve their TaxonomyEntry nodes that map to ATT&CK technique IDs.

queries: MATCH (n:SubTechnique) WHERE coalesce(n.attack_id, n.id) IN $ids OPTIONAL MATCH (n)-[r]-(m) WITH n, CASE WHEN m IS NULL THEN NULL ELSE type(r) END AS rel, CASE WHEN m IS NULL THEN NULL ELSE startNode(r) = n END AS outgoing, CASE WHEN m IS NULL THEN NULL ELSE head(labels(m)) END AS neighbour_label, count(m) AS cnt WITH n, collect(CASE WHEN rel IS NULL THEN NULL ELSE {rel: rel, outgoing: outgoing, label: neighbour_label, count: cnt} END) AS raw WITH n, [f IN raw WHERE f IS NOT NULL] AS facets RETURN coalesce(n.attack_id, n.id) AS id, n.name AS name, n.properties_json AS properties_json, facets AS facets LIMIT 1000

MATCH (t:Technique)-[:HAS_SUBTECHNIQUE]->(st:SubTechnique) WHERE t.attack_id IN $ids OR st.attack_id IN $ids RETURN t.attack_id AS parent_id, t.name AS parent_name, st.attack_id AS subtechnique_id, st.name AS subtechnique_name LIMIT 1000

CAPEC-16 (Dictionary-based Password Attack): An attacker tries each of the words in a dictionary as passwords to gain access to the system via some user's account. If the password chosen by the user was a word within the dictionary, this attack will be successful (in the absence of other mitigations). This is a specific instance of the password brute forcing attack pattern. Dictionary Attacks differ from similar attacks such as Password Spraying (CAPEC-565) and Credential Stuffing (CAPEC-600), since they leverage unknown username/password combinations and don't care about inducing account lockouts.

CAPEC-150 (Collect Data from Common Resource Locations) has Abstraction: Standard; Status: Draft; Typical_Severity: Medium.

CAPEC-150 (Collect Data from Common Resource Locations): An adversary exploits well-known locations for resources for the purposes of undermining the security of the target. In many, if not most systems, files and resources are organized in a default tree structure. This can be useful for adversaries because they often know where to look for resources or files that are necessary for attacks. Even when the precise location of a targeted resource may not be known, naming conventions may indicate a small area of the target machine's file tree where the resources are typically located. For example, configuration files are normally stored in the /etc director on Unix systems. Adversaries can take advantage of this to commit other types of attacks.

plan.text: Find all Techniques and SubTechniques whose names or descriptions relate to hijacking, stealing, or piggybacking on a legitimate session token, application access token, security token, or authentication material to impersonate a verified user or service (e.g., Use Alternate Authentication Material, Steal Application Access Token, and their sub-techniques such as Application Access Token, Security Token, OAuth Application Key).

For each Technique and SubTechnique identified in q1 (session-token hijacking / alternate authentication material), retrieve the Mitigations connected via the MITIGATES relationship, including the mitigation name and description, so a defender can see how to stop each behavior.

queries: MATCH (n) WHERE (n:Analytic OR n:Campaign OR n:DataComponent OR n:DetectionStrategy OR n:Group OR n:Matrix OR n:Mitigation OR n:Software OR n:SubTechnique OR n:Tactic OR n:Technique) AND any(term IN $names WHERE toLower(n.name) CONTAINS term) WITH collect(n) AS cand WITH cand, [x IN cand WHERE any(t IN $names WHERE toLower(x.name) = t)] AS exact UNWIND (CASE WHEN size(exact) > 0 THEN exact ELSE cand END) AS n OPTIONAL MATCH (n)-[r]-(m) WITH n, CASE WHEN m IS NULL THEN NULL ELSE type(r) END AS rel, CASE WHEN m IS NULL THEN NULL ELSE startNode(r) = n END AS outgoing, CASE WHEN m IS NULL THEN NULL ELSE head(labels(m)) END AS neighbour_label, count(m) AS cnt WITH n, collect(CASE WHEN rel IS NULL THEN NULL ELSE {rel: rel, outgoing: outgoing, label: neighbour_label, count: cnt} END) AS raw WITH n, [f IN raw WHERE f IS NOT NULL] AS facets RETURN coalesce(n.attack_id, n.id) AS id, n.name AS name, n.properties_json AS properties_json, facets AS facets LIMIT 1000

MATCH (n) WHERE (n:Analytic OR n:Campaign OR n:DataComponent OR n:DetectionStrategy OR n:Group OR n:Matrix OR n:Mitigation OR n:Software OR n:SubTechnique OR n:Tactic OR n:Technique) AND any(term IN $names WHERE toLower(n.name) CONTAINS term) WITH collect(n) AS cand WITH cand, [x IN cand WHERE any(t IN $names WHERE toLower(x.name) = t)] AS exact UNWIND (CASE WHEN size(exact) > 0 THEN exact ELSE cand END) AS n OPTIONAL MATCH (n)-[r]-(m) WITH n, CASE WHEN m IS NULL THEN NULL ELSE type(r) END AS rel, CASE WHEN m IS NULL THEN NULL ELSE startNode(r) = n END AS outgoing, CASE WHEN m IS NULL THEN NULL ELSE head(labels(m)) END AS neighbour_label, count(m) AS cnt WITH n, collect(CASE WHEN rel IS NULL THEN NULL ELSE {rel: rel, outgoing: outgoing, label: neighbour_label, count: cnt} END) AS raw WITH n, [f IN raw WHERE f IS NOT NULL] AS facets RETURN coalesce(n.attack_id, n.id) AS id, n.name AS name, n.properties_json AS properties_json, facets AS facets LIMIT 1000

MATCH (t:Technique) WHERE t.attack_id IN $ids OPTIONAL MATCH (t)<-[:MITIGATES]-(m:Mitigation) RETURN t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name, m.attack_id AS mitigation_id, m.name AS mitigation_name LIMIT 1000

MATCH (t:Technique) WHERE t.attack_id IN $ids OPTIONAL MATCH (t)<-[:MITIGATES]-(m:Mitigation) RETURN t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name, m.attack_id AS mitigation_id, m.name AS mitigation_name LIMIT 1000

MATCH (t:Technique)-[:HAS_SUBTECHNIQUE]->(st:SubTechnique) WHERE t.attack_id IN $ids OR st.attack_id IN $ids RETURN t.attack_id AS parent_id, t.name AS parent_name, st.attack_id AS subtechnique_id, st.name AS subtechnique_name LIMIT 1000

queries: MATCH (n) WHERE (n:Analytic OR n:Campaign OR n:DataComponent OR n:DetectionStrategy OR n:Group OR n:Matrix OR n:Mitigation OR n:Software OR n:SubTechnique OR n:Tactic OR n:Technique) AND any(term IN $names WHERE toLower(n.name) CONTAINS term) WITH collect(n) AS cand WITH cand, [x IN cand WHERE any(t IN $names WHERE toLower(x.name) = t)] AS exact UNWIND (CASE WHEN size(exact) > 0 THEN exact ELSE cand END) AS n OPTIONAL MATCH (n)-[r]-(m) WITH n, CASE WHEN m IS NULL THEN NULL ELSE type(r) END AS rel, CASE WHEN m IS NULL THEN NULL ELSE startNode(r) = n END AS outgoing, CASE WHEN m IS NULL THEN NULL ELSE head(labels(m)) END AS neighbour_label, count(m) AS cnt WITH n, collect(CASE WHEN rel IS NULL THEN NULL ELSE {rel: rel, outgoing: outgoing, label: neighbour_label, count: cnt} END) AS raw WITH n, [f IN raw WHERE f IS NOT NULL] AS facets RETURN coalesce(n.attack_id, n.id) AS id, n.name AS name, n.properties_json AS properties_json, facets AS facets LIMIT 1000

CAPEC-565 (Password Spraying): In a Password Spraying attack, an adversary tries a small list (e.g. 3-5) of common or expected passwords, often matching the target's complexity policy, against a known list of user accounts to gain valid credentials. plan.text: Find AttackPattern entries whose description involves exploiting a flaw in identity verification to fabricate or spoof an access credential that impersonates a different party, then attaching that fabricated credential to a running process so that a subsequent authorization or access decision is made based on the false identity. For each matching pattern, also retrieve its TaxonomyEntry mappings (via MAPS_TO) where the external taxonomy is ATT&CK, to obtain the corresponding ATT&CK technique identifiers.

For the ATT&CK Technique and SubTechnique nodes identified via the join, retrieve each node's associated Tactic(s) through the HAS_TACTIC relationship, returning the Tactic name and ID for every matched technique/sub-technique.

queries: MATCH (ta:Tactic)-[:HAS_TECHNIQUE]->(t) WHERE (t:Technique OR t:SubTechnique) AND t.attack_id IN $ids RETURN t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name, ta.attack_id AS in_tactic_id, ta.name AS in_tactic_name LIMIT 1000
g.V().hasLabel("AttackPattern").project("ap","tax").by(elementMap()).by(__.out("MAPS_TO").hasLabel("TaxonomyEntry").has("taxonomy_name","ATTACK").elementMap().fold()).limit(1000)

There are a great many ways in which the search space may be reduced.”; “Explore 3 [Expand victory conditions] It is sometimes possible to expand victory conditions. queries: MATCH (n:Mitigation) WHERE coalesce(n.attack_id, n.id) IN $ids RETURN coalesce(n.attack_id, n.id) AS id, n.name AS name LIMIT 200

MATCH (n:Technique) WHERE coalesce(n.attack_id, n.id) IN $ids OPTIONAL MATCH (n)-[r]-(m) WITH n, CASE WHEN m IS NULL THEN NULL ELSE type(r) END AS rel, CASE WHEN m IS NULL THEN NULL ELSE startNode(r) = n END AS outgoing, CASE WHEN m IS NULL THEN NULL ELSE head(labels(m)) END AS neighbour_label, count(m) AS cnt WITH n, collect(CASE WHEN rel IS NULL THEN NULL ELSE {rel: rel, outgoing: outgoing, label: neighbour_label, count: cnt} END) AS raw WITH n, [f IN raw WHERE f IS NOT NULL] AS facets RETURN coalesce(n.attack_id, n.id) AS id, n.name AS name, n.properties_json AS properties_json, facets AS facets LIMIT 50

MATCH (t) WHERE (t:Technique OR t:SubTechnique) AND t.attack_id IN $ids MATCH (t)<-[:DETECTS]-(d:DetectionStrategy) OPTIONAL MATCH (d)-[:HAS_ANALYTIC]->(a:Analytic) RETURN t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name, d.attack_id AS detection_id, d.name AS detection_name, a.attack_id AS analytic_id, a.name AS analytic_name LIMIT 200

MATCH (t:Technique) WHERE t.attack_id IN $ids MATCH (t)<-[:DETECTS]-(d:DetectionStrategy) OPTIONAL MATCH (d)-[:HAS_ANALYTIC]->(a:Analytic) RETURN t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name, d.attack_id AS detection_id, d.name AS detection_name, a.attack_id AS analytic_id, a.name AS analytic_name LIMIT 1000

MATCH (t:Technique)-[:HAS_SUBTECHNIQUE]->(st:SubTechnique) WHERE t.attack_id IN $ids OR st.attack_id IN $ids RETURN t.attack_id AS parent_id, t.name AS parent_name, st.attack_id AS subtechnique_id, st.name AS subtechnique_name LIMIT 1000

queries: MATCH (n:Technique) WHERE coalesce(n.attack_id, n.id) IN $ids OPTIONAL MATCH (n)-[r]-(m) WITH n, CASE WHEN m IS NULL THEN NULL ELSE type(r) END AS rel, CASE WHEN m IS NULL THEN NULL ELSE startNode(r) = n END AS outgoing, CASE WHEN m IS NULL THEN NULL ELSE head(labels(m)) END AS neighbour_label, count(m) AS cnt WITH n, collect(CASE WHEN rel IS NULL THEN NULL ELSE {rel: rel, outgoing: outgoing, label: neighbour_label, count: cnt} END) AS raw WITH n, [f IN raw WHERE f IS NOT NULL] AS facets RETURN coalesce(n.attack_id, n.id) AS id, n.name AS name, n.properties_json AS properties_json, facets AS facets LIMIT 20

MATCH (t:Technique)-[:HAS_SUBTECHNIQUE]->(st:SubTechnique) WHERE t.attack_id IN $ids OR st.attack_id IN $ids RETURN t.attack_id AS parent_id, t.name AS parent_name, st.attack_id AS subtechnique_id, st.name AS subtechnique_name LIMIT 1000

MATCH (t:Technique)-[:HAS_SUBTECHNIQUE]->(st:SubTechnique) WHERE t.attack_id IN $ids OR st.attack_id IN $ids RETURN t.attack_id AS parent_id, t.name AS parent_name, st.attack_id AS subtechnique_id, st.name AS subtechnique_name LIMIT 1000

MATCH (ta:Tactic)-[:HAS_TECHNIQUE]->(t) WHERE (t:Technique OR t:SubTechnique) AND t.attack_id IN $ids RETURN t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name, ta.attack_id AS in_tactic_id, ta.name AS in_tactic_name LIMIT 1000

For the ATT&CK Technique and SubTechnique nodes whose attack_id matches the IDs obtained from q2, retrieve all Mitigation nodes connected via MITIGATES, along with the mitigation names and descriptions.
For each AttackPattern identified in q1, retrieve all Mitigation nodes connected via HAS_MITIGATION, along with the mitigation descriptions.

plan.text: Find all AttackPattern nodes that have an EXPLOITS_WEAKNESS relationship to the Weakness node representing CWE-308 (Improper Handling of Case Sensitivity). Return the AttackPattern IDs and names.
For the AttackPatterns identified in q1, retrieve their MAPS_TO TaxonomyEntry nodes where the taxonomy is ATT&CK, to obtain the corresponding ATT&CK technique/sub-technique IDs (entry_id).

Retrieve the Technique and SubTechnique nodes whose attack_id matches the ATT&CK IDs produced by q2, and for each, retrieve associated Mitigation nodes via the MITIGATES relationship to identify defensive measures.
For the AttackPatterns identified in q1, retrieve their associated Mitigation nodes via the HAS_MITIGATION relationship to identify CAPEC-level countermeasures for CWE-308 exploitation.

queries: MATCH (t) WHERE (t:Technique OR t:SubTechnique) AND t.attack_id IN $ids OPTIONAL MATCH (t)<-[:MITIGATES]-(m:Mitigation) RETURN t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name, m.attack_id AS mitigation_id, m.name AS mitigation_name LIMIT 1000
g.V().has("id", within(ids)).project("ap","tax").by(elementMap()).by(__.out("MAPS_TO").hasLabel("TaxonomyEntry").has("taxonomy_name","ATTACK").elementMap().fold()).limit(1000)

CAPEC-3 (Using Leading 'Ghost' Character Sequences to Bypass Input Filters): Some APIs will strip certain leading characters from a string of parameters. An adversary can intentionally introduce leading "ghost" characters (extra characters that don't affect the validity of the request at the API layer) that enable the input to pass the filters and therefore process the adversary's input. This occurs when the targeted API will accept input data in several syntactic forms and interpret it in the equivalent semantic way, while the filter does not take into account the full spectrum of the syntactic forms acceptable to the targeted API.

claims: CAPEC-3 (Using Leading 'Ghost' Character Sequences to Bypass Input Filters) Likelihood Of Attack: Medium.

CAPEC-3 (Using Leading 'Ghost' Character Sequences to Bypass Input Filters) has 3 mitigations, named only as text: “Use an allowlist rather than a denylist input validation.”; “Canonicalize all data prior to validation.”; “Take an iterative approach to input validation (defense in depth).”.
CAPEC-3 (Using Leading 'Ghost' Character Sequences to Bypass Input Filters) has Abstraction: Detailed; Likelihood_Of_Attack: Medium; Status: Draft; Typical_Severity: Medium.

CAPEC-3 (Using Leading 'Ghost' Character Sequences to Bypass Input Filters): Some APIs will strip certain leading characters from a string of parameters. An adversary can intentionally introduce leading "ghost" characters (extra characters that don't affect the validity of the request at the API layer) that enable the input to pass the filters and therefore process the adversary's input. This occurs when the targeted API will accept input data in several syntactic forms and interpret it in the equivalent semantic way, while the filter does not take into account the full spectrum of the syntactic forms acceptable to the targeted API.

claims: CAPEC-1 (Accessing Functionality Not Properly Constrained by ACLs) description: In applications, particularly web applications, access to functionality is mitigated by an authorization framework. This framework maps Access Control Lists (ACLs) to elements of the application's functionality; particularly URL's for web apps. In the case that the administrator failed to specify an ACL for a particular element, an attacker may be able to access it with impunity. An attacker with the ability to access functionality not properly constrained by ACLs can obtain sensitive information and possibly compromise the entire application. Such an attacker can access resources that must be available only to users at a higher privilege level, can access management sections of the application, or can run queries for data that they otherwise not supposed to..

CAPEC-62 (Cross Site Request Forgery) description: An attacker crafts malicious web links and distributes them (via web pages, email, etc.), typically in a targeted manner, hoping to induce users to click on the link and execute the malicious action against some third-party application. This type of attack leverages the persistence and implicit trust placed in user session cookies by many web applications today. In such an architecture, once the user authenticates to an application and a session cookie is created on the user's system, all following transactions for that session are authenticated using that cookie including potential actions initiated by an attacker and simply "riding" the existing session cookie..

Note that this attack is applicable to VOIP data as well as application data, especially for interactive apps that require precise timing and low-latency (e.g. thin-clients)..

CAPEC-622 (Electromagnetic Side-Channel Attack) description: In this attack scenario, the attacker passively monitors electromagnetic emanations that are produced by the targeted electronic device as an unintentional side-effect of its processing. From these emanations, the attacker derives information about the data that is being processed (e.g. the attacker can recover cryptographic keys by monitoring emanations associated with cryptographic processing). This style of attack requires proximal access to the device, however attacks have been demonstrated at public conferences that work at distances of up to 10-15 feet. There have not been any significant studies to determine the maximum practical distance for such attacks. Since the attack is passive, it is nearly impossible to detect and the targeted device will continue to operate as normal after a successful attack..

CAPEC-623 (Compromising Emanations Attack) description: Compromising Emanations (CE) are defined as unintentional signals which an attacker may intercept and analyze to disclose the information processed by the targeted equipment. Commercial mobile devices and retransmission devices have displays, buttons, microchips, and radios that emit mechanical emissions in the form of sound or vibrations. Capturing these emissions can help an adversary understand what the device is doing..

Return strategy IDs, analytic IDs, and data-component names.

Find AttackPattern nodes whose names, descriptions, or AlternateTerm nodes match 'password guessing', 'dictionary attack', 'brute force password', or 'credential brute force'. Also retrieve any Category they belong to via MEMBER_OF. Return pattern IDs, names, and category names.

For the password-guessing / dictionary-attack AttackPattern(s) identified in q4, retrieve all Mitigation nodes via HAS_MITIGATION, all Indicator nodes via HAS_INDICATOR, and all Prerequisite nodes via HAS_PREREQUISITE. Return their IDs, names, and descriptions.

There are many attack vectors for XSS on the client side and the server side. CAPEC-63 (Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)): An adversary embeds malicious scripts in content that will be served to web browsers. The goal of the attack is for the target software, the client-side browser, to execute the script with the users' privilege level. An attack of this type exploits a programs' vulnerabilities that are brought on by allowing remote hosts to execute code and scripts. Web browsers, for example, have some simple security controls in place, but if a remote attacker is allowed to execute scripts (through injecting them in to user-generated content like bulletin boards) then these controls may be bypassed. Further, these attacks are very difficult for an end user to detect.

plan.text: Find Techniques and SubTechniques that describe adversary behaviors of accessing a system remotely via RDP, SSH, telnet, or VNC using stolen or valid login credentials. Include the parent Tactic for each. Focus on techniques such as Remote Desktop Protocol, Remote Services, Valid Accounts, and any sub-techniques that specify these channels or credential-based authentication.

Find all Mitigations that MITIGATES the Techniques and SubTechniques identified in q1 (remote access via RDP/SSH/telnet/VNC using stolen or valid credentials). Return the mitigation name, description, and the technique it mitigates.

Find AttackPatterns that describe an adversary using stolen or compromised login credentials to gain access to a system through remote channels such as RDP, SSH, telnet, or VNC. For each matching pattern, retrieve its associated Mitigations (countermeasures) via HAS_MITIGATION, and any Prerequisites or Resources that specify the credential or channel requirement.

claims: CAPEC-1 (Accessing Functionality Not Properly Constrained by ACLs) description: In applications, particularly web applications, access to functionality is mitigated by an authorization framework. This framework maps Access Control Lists (ACLs) to elements of the application's functionality; particularly URL's for web apps. In the case that the administrator failed to specify an ACL for a particular element, an attacker may be able to access it with impunity. An attacker with the ability to access functionality not properly constrained by ACLs can obtain sensitive information and possibly compromise the entire application. Such an attacker can access resources that must be available only to users at a higher privilege level, can access management sections of the application, or can run queries for data that they otherwise not supposed to..

CAPEC-10 (Buffer Overflow via Environment Variables) description: This attack pattern involves causing a buffer overflow through manipulation of environment variables. Once the adversary finds that they can modify an environment variable, they may try to overflow associated buffers. This attack leverages implicit trust often placed in environment variables..

CAPEC-100 (Overflow Buffers) description: Buffer Overflow attacks target improper or missing bounds checking on buffer operations, typically triggered by input injected by an adversary. As a consequence, an adversary is able to write past the boundaries of allocated buffer regions in memory, causing a program crash or potentially redirection of execution as per the adversaries' choice..

CAPEC-101 (Server Side Include (SSI) Injection) description: An attacker can use Server Side Include (SSI) Injection to send code to a web application that then gets executed by the web server. Doing so enables the attacker to achieve similar results to Cross Site Scripting, viz., arbitrary code execution and information disclosure, albeit on a more limited scale, since the SSI directives are nowhere near as powerful as a full-fledged scripting language. Nonetheless, the attacker can conveniently gain access to sensitive files, such as password files, and execute shell commands..

CAPEC-62 (Cross Site Request Forgery) description: An attacker crafts malicious web links and distributes them (via web pages, email, etc.), typically in a targeted manner, hoping to induce users to click on the link and execute the malicious action against some third-party application. If successful, the action embedded in the malicious link will be processed and accepted by the targeted application with the users' privilege level. This type of attack leverages the persistence and implicit trust placed in user session cookies by many web applications today. In such an architecture, once the user authenticates to an application and a session cookie is created on the user's system, all following transactions for that session are authenticated using that cookie including potential actions initiated by an attacker and simply "riding" the existing session cookie..
CAPEC-620 (Drop Encryption Level) description: An attacker forces the encryption level to be lowered, thus enabling a successful attack against the encrypted data..

CAPEC-621 (Analysis of Packet Timing and Sizes) description: An attacker may intercept and log encrypted transmissions for the purpose of analyzing metadata such as packet timing and sizes. Although the actual data may be encrypted, this metadata may reveal valuable information to an attacker. Note that this attack is applicable to VOIP data as well as application data, especially for interactive apps that require precise timing and low-latency (e.g. thin-clients)..

CAPEC-622 (Electromagnetic Side-Channel Attack) description: In this attack scenario, the attacker passively monitors electromagnetic emanations that are produced by the targeted electronic device as an unintentional side-effect of its processing. From these emanations, the attacker derives information about the data that is being processed (e.g. the attacker can recover cryptographic keys by monitoring emanations associated with cryptographic processing). This style of attack requires proximal access to the device, however attacks have been demonstrated at public conferences that work at distances of up to 10-15 feet. There have not been any significant studies to determine the maximum practical distance for such attacks. Since the attack is passive, it is nearly impossible to detect and the targeted device will continue to operate as normal after a successful attack..

CAPEC-623 (Compromising Emanations Attack) description: Compromising Emanations (CE) are defined as unintentional signals which an attacker may intercept and analyze to disclose the information processed by the targeted equipment. Commercial mobile devices and retransmission devices have displays, buttons, microchips, and radios that emit mechanical emissions in the form of sound or vibrations. Capturing these emissions can help an adversary understand what the device is doing..

CAPEC-624 (Hardware Fault Injection) description: The adversary uses disruptive signals or events, or alters the physical environment a device operates in, to cause faulty behavior in electronic devices. This can include electromagnetic pulses, laser pulses, clock glitches, ambient temperature extremes, and more. When performed in a controlled manner on devices performing cryptographic operations, this faulty behavior can be exploited to derive secret key information..

plan.text: Find the AttackPatterns named 'Embedding Scripts within Scripts', 'Leverage Executable Code in Non-Executable Files', and 'Embed Virus into DLL'; for each, traverse MAPS_TO to TaxonomyEntry where the taxonomy is ATTACK, and return the entry_id values (ATT&CK technique IDs).

For the deduplicated set of ATT&CK technique IDs received from the CAPEC mapping, locate the corresponding Technique and SubTechnique nodes, then traverse MITIGATES to retrieve all associated Mitigations. Return the deduplicated union of mitigations across all matched techniques.

queries: MATCH (t) WHERE (t:Technique OR t:SubTechnique) AND t.attack_id IN $ids OPTIONAL MATCH (t)<-[:MITIGATES]-(m:Mitigation) RETURN t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name, m.attack_id AS mitigation_id, m.name AS mitigation_name LIMIT 1000
g.V().hasLabel("AttackPattern").project("ap","tax").by(elementMap()).by(__.out("MAPS_TO").hasLabel("TaxonomyEntry").has("taxonomy_name","ATTACK").elementMap().fold()).limit(1000)

Return the technique IDs, names, and any relevant sub-technique IDs for each.", query='MATCH (n:Technique) WHERE coalesce(n.attack_id, n.id) IN $ids RETURN coalesce(n.attack_id, n.id) AS id, n.name AS name LIMIT 1000')

gold_question: Which ATT&CK techniques do CAPEC-19, CAPEC-35, CAPEC-448 map to (they overlap), and what mitigations apply to the deduplicated union?
note: paraphrased all three names' ideas, no identifiers/names/avoid words

plan.text: Identify the Technique and SubTechnique entries that correspond to each of these three described adversary behaviors: (1) hiding or inserting one script inside another script so it executes covertly alongside the host script; (2) embedding executable or runnable code inside files that are not designed to execute code (e.g., image files, configuration files); (3) embedding malicious code in unused or leftover padding space within the instruction stream of a compiled library or binary. Return the technique IDs, names, and any relevant sub-technique IDs for each.

For every Technique and SubTechnique identified in q1, retrieve all Mitigation nodes connected via the MITIGATES relationship, so the results form a combined, de-duplicated set of ATT&CK countermeasures covering all three described behaviors.

Find all AttackPattern nodes whose MAPS_TO relationship points to a TaxonomyEntry with taxonomy=ATTACK and an entry_id matching any technique or sub-technique id returned in q1. For each matching AttackPattern, also retrieve its Mitigation nodes via HAS_MITIGATION, to supplement the ATT&CK mitigation set with CAPEC-level countermeasures.

queries: MATCH (n:Technique) WHERE coalesce(n.attack_id, n.id) IN $ids RETURN coalesce(n.attack_id, n.id) AS id, n.name AS name LIMIT 1000

MATCH (t) WHERE (t:Technique OR t:SubTechnique) AND t.attack_id IN $ids OPTIONAL MATCH (t)<-[:MITIGATES]-(m:Mitigation) RETURN t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name, m.attack_id AS mitigation_id, m.name AS mitigation_name LIMIT 1000
g.V().hasLabel("AttackPattern").project("ap","tax").by(elementMap()).by(__.out("MAPS_TO").hasLabel("TaxonomyEntry").has("taxonomy_name","ATTACK").elementMap().fold()).limit(1000)
question: Since these three approaches overlap — hiding one script inside another so it quietly runs too, sneaking runnable code into files that aren't meant to run any code themselves (like an image or configuration file), and slipping a virus into leftover padding inside a compiled library's instructions — which adversary behaviors would each line up with, and what combined set of countermeasures would help?

plan.text: Identify the three CAPEC attack patterns matching: (1) a script hidden inside another script that a target program is likely to execute, enabled by a remote-code-execution flaw; (2) exploitation of a system's trust in its own configuration or resource files so that loading an altered image or settings file causes hidden code to run or the running process to be hijacked; (3) tampering with a compiled shared library by planting a virus in the padding gaps left between legitimate instructions by compiler optimizations, so that any consumer of that library becomes infected. Return each pattern's ExecutionSteps, Prerequisites, Resources, Skills, Weaknesses, Indicators, and Consequences.
For the three attack patterns identified in q1, retrieve all associated Mitigation nodes (countermeasures and defensive recommendations) and any ExternalReference nodes that cite published guidance.

Find the ATT&CK Technique and SubTechnique nodes whose attack_id values correspond to the CAPEC attack patterns resolved in q1 (via the declared attack-technique-id mapping). Return each technique's parent Tactic and any HAS_SUBTECHNIQUE children so the full adversary-behavior context is visible.

For the ATT&CK techniques and sub-techniques identified in q3, retrieve all Mitigation nodes linked via MITIGATES, including the mitigation description and any associated DataComponent or Analytic that operationalises the mitigation.

For the ATT&CK techniques and sub-techniques identified in q3, retrieve all DetectionStrategy nodes linked via DETECTS and their associated Analytic and DataComponent children, so the analyst can see how each adversary behavior can be detected in practice.

claims: CAPEC-1 (Accessing Functionality Not Properly Constrained by ACLs) description: In applications, particularly web applications, access to functionality is mitigated by an authorization framework. This framework maps Access Control Lists (ACLs) to elements of the application's functionality; particularly URL's for web apps. In the case that the administrator failed to specify an ACL for a particular element, an attacker may be able to access it with impunity. An attacker with the ability to access functionality not properly constrained by ACLs can obtain sensitive information and possibly compromise the entire application. Such an attacker can access resources that must be available only to users at a higher privilege level, can access management sections of the application, or can run queries for data that they otherwise not supposed to..
CAPEC-1 (Accessing Functionality Not Properly Constrained by ACLs) has 1 ATT&CK mapping: T1574.010.

CAPEC-10 (Buffer Overflow via Environment Variables) description: This attack pattern involves causing a buffer overflow through manipulation of environment variables. Once the adversary finds that they can modify an environment variable, they may try to overflow associated buffers. This attack leverages implicit trust often placed in environment variables..

CAPEC-100 (Overflow Buffers) description: Buffer Overflow attacks target improper or missing bounds checking on buffer operations, typically triggered by input injected by an adversary. As a consequence, an adversary is able to write past the boundaries of allocated buffer regions in memory, causing a program crash or potentially redirection of execution as per the adversaries' choice..

CAPEC-101 (Server Side Include (SSI) Injection) description: An attacker can use Server Side Include (SSI) Injection to send code to a web application that then gets executed by the web server. Doing so enables the attacker to achieve similar results to Cross Site Scripting, viz., arbitrary code execution and information disclosure, albeit on a more limited scale, since the SSI directives are nowhere near as powerful as a full-fledged scripting language. Nonetheless, the attacker can conveniently gain access to sensitive files, such as password files, and execute shell commands..
CAPEC-11 (Cause Web Server Misclassification) has 1 ATT&CK mapping: T1036.006.
CAPEC-112 (Brute Force) has 1 ATT&CK mapping: T1110.
CAPEC-114 (Authentication Abuse) has 1 ATT&CK mapping: T1548.
CAPEC-115 (Authentication Bypass) has 1 ATT&CK mapping: T1548.

CAPEC-62 (Cross Site Request Forgery) description: An attacker crafts malicious web links and distributes them (via web pages, email, etc.), typically in a targeted manner, hoping to induce users to click on the link and execute the malicious action against some third-party application. If successful, the action embedded in the malicious link will be processed and accepted by the targeted application with the users' privilege level. This type of attack leverages the persistence and implicit trust placed in user session cookies by many web applications today. In such an architecture, once the user authenticates to an application and a session cookie is created on the user's system, all following transactions for that session are authenticated using that cookie including potential actions initiated by an attacker and simply "riding" the existing session cookie..
CAPEC-620 (Drop Encryption Level) description: An attacker forces the encryption level to be lowered, thus enabling a successful attack against the encrypted data..
CAPEC-620 (Drop Encryption Level) has 1 ATT&CK mapping: T1600.

CAPEC-621 (Analysis of Packet Timing and Sizes) description: An attacker may intercept and log encrypted transmissions for the purpose of analyzing metadata such as packet timing and sizes. Although the actual data may be encrypted, this metadata may reveal valuable information to an attacker. Note that this attack is applicable to VOIP data as well as application data, especially for interactive apps that require precise timing and low-latency (e.g. thin-clients)..

CAPEC-622 (Electromagnetic Side-Channel Attack) description: In this attack scenario, the attacker passively monitors electromagnetic emanations that are produced by the targeted electronic device as an unintentional side-effect of its processing. From these emanations, the attacker derives information about the data that is being processed (e.g. the attacker can recover cryptographic keys by monitoring emanations associated with cryptographic processing). This style of attack requires proximal access to the device, however attacks have been demonstrated at public conferences that work at distances of up to 10-15 feet. There have not been any significant studies to determine the maximum practical distance for such attacks. Since the attack is passive, it is nearly impossible to detect and the targeted device will continue to operate as normal after a successful attack..

CAPEC-623 (Compromising Emanations Attack) description: Compromising Emanations (CE) are defined as unintentional signals which an attacker may intercept and analyze to disclose the information processed by the targeted equipment. Commercial mobile devices and retransmission devices have displays, buttons, microchips, and radios that emit mechanical emissions in the form of sound or vibrations. Capturing these emissions can help an adversary understand what the device is doing..

CAPEC-624 (Hardware Fault Injection) description: The adversary uses disruptive signals or events, or alters the physical environment a device operates in, to cause faulty behavior in electronic devices. This can include electromagnetic pulses, laser pulses, clock glitches, ambient temperature extremes, and more. When performed in a controlled manner on devices performing cryptographic operations, this faulty behavior can be exploited to derive secret key information..

plan.text: Find Technique and SubTechnique nodes that describe an adversary quietly modifying environment variables or environment settings that a program depends on, causing the program to behave in the adversary's favor (e.g., T1562.006 Environment Variable, T1542.001 Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder). Return the technique name, id, and its parent Tactic via HAS_TACTIC.

Find Technique and SubTechnique nodes that describe injecting or loading code into the memory space of an already-running, separate process by exploiting a program's failure to verify that process's integrity (e.g., T1055 Process Injection, T1055.001 Dynamic Code Loading, T1055.002 Portable Executable Injection, T1055.003 Thread Execution Hijacking). Return the technique name, id, and its parent Tactic via HAS_TACTIC.

Find AttackPattern nodes whose description involves an adversary manipulating or altering environment settings, configuration variables, or runtime parameters that a target program relies on, to redirect its behavior. Include any linked Mitigation nodes via HAS_MITIGATION and any linked Weakness nodes via EXPLOITS_WEAKNESS.

Find AttackPattern nodes whose description involves injecting code or data into the memory space of a separate, already-running process, or exploiting a program's failure to validate the integrity of another process's memory (e.g., process injection, DLL hijacking, memory corruption). Include any linked Mitigation nodes via HAS_MITIGATION and any linked Weakness nodes via EXPLOITS_WEAKNESS.

For the techniques and sub-techniques identified in q1 and q2 (environment-variable manipulation and process/memory injection), retrieve all Mitigation nodes connected via the MITIGATES relationship. Return mitigation name, id, and description.

For the AttackPattern nodes identified in q3 and q4 (environment manipulation and process/memory injection), retrieve all Mitigation nodes connected via the HAS_MITIGATION relationship. Return mitigation name and description.

queries: MATCH (t) WHERE (t:Technique OR t:SubTechnique) AND t.attack_id IN $ids OPTIONAL MATCH (t)<-[:MITIGATES]-(m:Mitigation) RETURN t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name, m.attack_id AS mitigation_id, m.name AS mitigation_name LIMIT 100

plan.text: Identify the Technique or SubTechnique that describes an adversary modifying environment variables or runtime configuration settings that a running program reads, causing the program to deviate from its intended behavior and act in favor of the modifier. Retrieve the matching Technique/SubTechnique node(s) and all Mitigation nodes connected via MITIGATES.

Identify the Technique or SubTechnique that describes an adversary exploiting a program's failure to validate the legitimacy of a separate already-running process, then injecting external instructions or code into that process's memory space to gain access to resources within its address space. Retrieve the matching Technique/SubTechnique node(s) and all Mitigation nodes connected via MITIGATES.

Identify the AttackPattern that describes an adversary manipulating environment variables or runtime configuration parameters that a running application reads, causing the application to deviate from its intended behavior. Retrieve the AttackPattern, its ExecutionSteps, any Mitigation nodes linked via HAS_MITIGATION, and any TaxonomyEntry linked via MAPS_TO (especially those mapping to the ATT&CK taxonomy).

Identify the AttackPattern that describes an adversary exploiting a program's failure to verify the legitimacy of a separate running process and injecting external code or instructions into that process's memory space to access resources within its address space. Retrieve the AttackPattern, its ExecutionSteps, any Mitigation nodes linked via HAS_MITIGATION, and any TaxonomyEntry linked via MAPS_TO (especially those mapping to the ATT&CK taxonomy).

question: Picture two separate tricks that overlap here: one quietly edits the settings a running program reads from its environment so the program starts behaving in a way that favors whoever changed them, deviating from what it was meant to do; the other takes advantage of a program's failure to confirm that a separate, already-running process is still legitimate, then slips outside instructions into that process's own memory space, potentially reaching whatever resources happen to be within reach — which adversary behaviors would each line up with, and what combined set of countermeasures would help?

Expected matches include the Unsecured Credentials family (T1552 and sub-techniques) and OS Credential Dumping (T1003).

Find all Techniques and SubTechniques that describe the adversary behavior of searching through files or data stores that an application left without proper access controls in order to locate hidden sensitive information. Expected matches include Data from Local System (T1005), Data from Information Repositories (T1213), and related collection/exfiltration techniques.

Retrieve all Mitigation nodes that MITIGATES any Technique or SubTechnique identified in q1 (Unsecured Credentials / OS Credential Dumping family) or q2 (Data from Local System / Data from Information Repositories family). Return the mitigation name, description, and the specific technique(s) it mitigates so the combined countermeasure set can be assembled.

Find CAPEC AttackPattern nodes whose TaxonomyEntry (taxonomy = ATTACK) maps to the ATT&CK technique IDs identified in q1 and q2 (e.g., T1552, T1552.001, T1003, T1005, T1213). For each matching AttackPattern, also retrieve its associated Mitigation nodes (via HAS_MITIGATION) to capture CAPEC-specific countermeasures that complement the ATT&CK mitigations.
